subject: Agriculture
title: Phylloxera and Wine
description: A 60-second lesson on Phylloxera and Wine.

hook.text: In the 1860s, a tiny insect from America nearly destroyed every vineyard in Europe. Wine itself almost died.

buildup.text: Phylloxera—a root-feeding aphid—hitchhiked on American vine imports. European vines had no resistance.

discovery.text: Within 30 years, phylloxera destroyed 70% of France's vineyards. The wine industry faced total collapse.

twist.text: The solution: graft European vines onto resistant American rootstock. Nearly all wine today still grows this way.

climax.text: Phylloxera taught agriculture that genetic diversity is insurance. Monocultures invite catastrophe.

punchline.text: French wine survives on American roots. The pest created a permanent marriage.

quiz.question: How was the phylloxera crisis in European vineyards solved?
options: Grafting European vines onto resistant American rootstock

details.summary: Phylloxera is a tiny sap-feeding insect native to North America that devastated European vineyards in the late 1800s, destroying two-thirds of all European grapevines. The solution—grafting European vines onto resistant American rootstocks—saved the wine industry and is still used today.
details.whyItMatters: The phylloxera crisis nearly destroyed the global wine industry and remains the most economically significant insect pest event in agricultural history.
takeaways: Phylloxera destroyed two-thirds of European vineyards between the 1860s and 1890s
Grafting European vines onto resistant American rootstocks saved the wine industry
Nearly all wine grapes worldwide today are grown on grafted American rootstocks

faq.question: How did phylloxera nearly destroy the European wine industry?
faq.answer: Phylloxera, accidentally introduced from North America, feeds on grapevine roots, causing them to rot. European grapevines (Vitis vinifera) had no evolutionary defense. The insect spread across France, then Europe, destroying millions of hectares of vineyards within 30 years.

faq.question: How was the phylloxera crisis eventually solved?
faq.answer: American grapevine species had coevolved resistance to phylloxera. The solution was grafting European wine grape varieties onto American rootstocks that resist the insect's feeding damage. This technique saved the industry and remains the standard practice in virtually all wine regions.
